title: Commas
blurb: Place every required comma and remove every wrong one: FANBOYS, introductions, nonessential elements, series, adjectives, dates and addresses.
question: A discharge note reads, “When the patient woke up the nurse, who was on duty checked his vital signs, and called the doctor.” Which commas are missing, which are wrong, and which rules decide?

teach.body: Formally, a comma marks a boundary inside a sentence: it separates independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, items in a series and coordinate adjectives, and it sets off introductory and nonessential elements. Plain English: a comma is never decoration. Each one has a job from a short list, and a comma with no job is an error. The TEAS shows four versions of one sentence; usually only one comma rule differs.

head: Job
Example
rows: The clinic opened, but the lab stayed closed.
When the shift ended, she went home.
Mr. Ruiz, your test is ready, isn't it?
teach.caption: The final comma before “and” in a series is a style choice; the TEAS will not hinge on it.

rows.label: Example
values: The nurse checked the chart, and the doctor called.
The nurse checked the chart and called the doctor.

teach.caption: Test: cover the part after the conjunction. If what follows can stand alone with its own subject, use a comma.

rows.label: Clause
values: The patient who fell needs an X-ray.
The clinic, which opened in 2020, is busy.

teach.caption: Nonessential elements need commas on BOTH sides unless they end the sentence.

rows.label: The new nurse on nights, works weekends.
I stayed late, because I was needed.
She was tired but, she stayed.
The bus was late, we missed it.

teach.note: Coordinate adjectives pass the “and” test (a long and tiring shift); cumulative ones fail it (a bright and red car).

teach.body: Keisha Brown, a nursing applicant, fixes: “When the patient woke up, the nurse, who was on duty, checked his vital signs and called the doctor.” The opening “When” clause is introductory, so it takes a comma. “Who was on duty” is extra information about the one nurse, so it needs a comma on both sides. “Checked ... and called” shares one subject, so the comma before “and” goes.

steps.label: Clauses joined?
steps.sub: Comma before FANBOYS only if both stand alone

steps.label: Introduction?
steps.sub: Comma after an opening clause or phrase

steps.label: Extra info?
steps.sub: Pair of commas around nonessential parts

teach.text: The top TEAS comma traps: a comma before “and” that joins two verbs with one subject, a missing comma after an introductory “When/Because/After” clause, only one comma of a nonessential pair, commas around an essential clause, and a comma between a long subject and its verb.

items: Comma + FANBOYS joins two independent clauses; no comma for one subject with two verbs.
Put a comma after an introductory clause, participial phrase or transition word.
Nonessential elements take a pair of commas; essential elements take none.
Comma between coordinate adjectives (long, tiring), not cumulative ones (bright red).
Never put a comma between a subject and its verb or after a conjunction.

summary: You can now apply each required comma rule and spot the common comma errors, from FANBOYS clauses and introductions to nonessential elements, adjectives, dates and places. You can also check four versions of a sentence quickly by testing subjects, verbs and removable information.

options: The nurse checked the chart, and the doctor reviewed the labs.
The nurse checked the chart and, the doctor reviewed the labs.
The nurse checked the chart and the doctor, reviewed the labs.
The nurse, checked the chart and the doctor reviewed the labs.
A.why: Two independent clauses joined by “and” take a comma before the conjunction.

whyNot.1: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.
whyNot.2: This comma splits the subject “the doctor” from its verb “reviewed.”
whyNot.3: This comma splits the subject “The nurse” from its verb “checked.”

A.q: Which version of the sentence about the end of a shift is punctuated correctly?
options: When the shift ended the nurses, gave their report.
When the shift ended the nurses gave their report.
When the shift ended, the nurses gave their report.
When, the shift ended the nurses gave their report.
A.why: An introductory dependent clause (“When the shift ended”) is followed by a comma.

whyNot.0: The comma splits the subject “the nurses” from its verb “gave,” and the introductory clause has none.
whyNot.1: Without a comma it reads as “the shift ended the nurses”; the introductory clause needs a comma.
whyNot.3: A comma cannot separate “When” from the rest of its own clause.

A.q: Which sentence about Mr. Diaz is punctuated correctly?
options: Mr. Diaz signed the form, and handed it to the clerk.
Mr. Diaz signed, the form and handed it to the clerk.
Mr. Diaz, signed the form and handed it to the clerk.
Mr. Diaz signed the form and handed it to the clerk.
A.why: One subject with two verbs (signed and handed) is a compound predicate, which takes no comma.

whyNot.0: “Handed it to the clerk” has no subject of its own, so no comma before “and.”
whyNot.1: A comma cannot split the verb “signed” from its object “the form.”
whyNot.2: A comma cannot split the subject “Mr. Diaz” from the verb “signed.”

B.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates the appositive?
options: Dr. Kim the new surgeon, arrived early.
Dr. Kim, the new surgeon, arrived early.
Dr. Kim, the new surgeon arrived early.
Dr. Kim, the new, surgeon arrived early.
B.why: “The new surgeon” is nonessential extra information about Dr. Kim, so it takes a comma on both sides.

whyNot.0: The opening comma of the pair is missing.
whyNot.2: The closing comma of the pair is missing.
whyNot.3: The second comma falls inside the appositive instead of after it, so the pair is broken.

B.q: Three patients share a room, and only one of them fell during the night. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The patient, who fell during the night, needs an X-ray.
The patient, who fell during the night needs an X-ray.
The patient who fell during the night, needs an X-ray.
The patient who fell during the night needs an X-ray.
B.why: With three patients, “who fell during the night” identifies which one, so it is essential and takes no commas.

whyNot.0: Commas mark the clause as extra information, but here it is needed to identify the patient.
whyNot.1: The clause is essential, and a single comma also separates the subject from its verb.
whyNot.2: This comma separates the full subject from its verb “needs.”

B.q: Which sentence punctuates its adjectives correctly?
options: After a long, tiring shift, she drove her bright red car home.
After a long tiring shift, she drove her bright, red car home.
After a long, tiring, shift, she drove her bright red car home.
After a long tiring shift she drove her bright, red car home.
B.why: Long and tiring are coordinate (a long and tiring shift), so they take a comma; bright red is cumulative, so it does not.

whyNot.1: Long and tiring are coordinate adjectives and need a comma, and bright modifies red, so “bright, red” is wrong.
whyNot.2: No comma goes between the last adjective and its noun (“tiring, shift”).
whyNot.3: Long and tiring are coordinate adjectives and need a comma, and “bright, red” wrongly splits the cumulative bright red.

C.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates the date and the place?
options: On July 4, 2026 the clinic in Austin, Texas opened.
On July 4 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened.
On July, 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin Texas, opened.
C.why: A full date takes commas after the day and after the year; a city-state pair takes commas after the city and after the state when the sentence continues.

whyNot.0: The commas after 2026 and after Texas are missing.
whyNot.1: The comma between the day and the year is missing.
whyNot.3: No comma goes between the month and the day, and one belongs between Austin and Texas.

C.q: Which sentence spoken to a patient is punctuated correctly?
options: Ms. Chen your test is scheduled for Monday, isn't it?
Ms. Chen, your test is scheduled for Monday, isn't it?
Ms. Chen, your test is scheduled for Monday isn't it?
Ms. Chen, your test, is scheduled for Monday, isn't it?
C.why: A name in direct address is set off by a comma, and so is a tag question.

whyNot.0: The comma after the name in direct address is missing.
whyNot.2: The tag question “isn't it” needs a comma before it.
whyNot.3: The comma after “test” splits the subject from its verb.

C.q: Which sentence contains a comma ERROR?
options: The new nurse on the night shift, works every weekend.
However, the night shift still needs two more nurses this month.
She needs rest, not more medication.
Yes, the lab results arrived this morning.
C.why: “The new nurse on the night shift” is the subject and “works” is its verb; no comma goes between them.

whyNot.1: A transition word that opens a sentence is followed by a comma.
whyNot.2: A contrasting element (“not more medication”) is set off by a comma.
whyNot.3: An introductory word such as “Yes” is followed by a comma.

reteach.title: Commas are traffic signs, not speed bumps
reteach.question: Think of each comma as a road sign that must have a reason to be there. What happens if you put a sign in the middle of a lane for no reason?

blocks.body: A real road has signs at junctions (FANBOYS joining two clauses), at on-ramps (introductions) and around detours (nonessential extras you could skip). A sign in the middle of a straight lane, between a subject and its verb, just causes a crash. So do not add a comma because you would pause when speaking; add it only when one of the rules gives it a job.

head: Spot on the road
Comma?
rows: One driver, two turns: two verbs, one subject

blocks.text: A pause in speech is not a rule. Long subjects often make people pause before the verb, but a comma there is always an error.

explain.body: Use a comma before for, and, nor, but, or, yet or so only when both sides are independent clauses with their own subjects. One subject with two verbs takes no comma.

test.q: Which sentence NEEDS a comma before its conjunction?
options: The aide washed her hands carefully and put on gloves.
The aide washed her hands but did not dry them.
The aide checked the pulse and recorded it.
The aide checked the pulse and the nurse recorded it.
test.why: “The nurse recorded it” has its own subject and verb, so two independent clauses are joined: comma before “and.”

whyNot.0: “Put on gloves” shares the subject “The aide,” so no comma.
whyNot.1: “Did not dry them” shares the subject, so no comma.
whyNot.2: “Recorded it” shares the subject, so no comma.

explain.body: Put a comma after an opening dependent clause (When..., Because...), a participial phrase (Exhausted by the shift,...), a long prepositional phrase, or a transition word (However, Yes).

test.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates its introductory phrase?
options: Exhausted by the double shift the nurse, slept.
Exhausted by the double shift, the nurse slept.
Exhausted, by the double shift the nurse slept.
Exhausted by the double shift; the nurse slept.
test.why: The participial phrase “Exhausted by the double shift” is introductory, so a comma follows it.

whyNot.0: The comma separates the subject “the nurse” from its verb.
whyNot.2: The comma breaks the phrase in the middle instead of ending it.
whyNot.3: A semicolon cannot follow a phrase; it joins independent clauses.

explain.body: If removing the words leaves the meaning intact, they are nonessential: enclose them in a pair of commas. If they identify which one you mean, they are essential: no commas.

test.q: The clause in this sentence is nonessential. Which version punctuates it correctly?
options: The clinic which opened in 2020, is busy.
The clinic, which opened in 2020 is busy.
The clinic, which opened in 2020, is busy.
The clinic which, opened in 2020, is busy.
test.why: A nonessential clause in the middle of a sentence is enclosed by a comma on each side.

whyNot.0: The opening comma of the pair is missing.
whyNot.1: The closing comma of the pair is missing.
whyNot.3: The first comma falls after “which,” splitting the clause itself.

explain.body: Separate three or more items in a series with commas. Separate coordinate adjectives (they pass the “and” test). Never put a comma after a conjunction, before the first item, or between cumulative adjectives such as “three large boxes.”

test.q: Which request for supplies is punctuated correctly?
options: Please bring gauze, tape, and three large boxes.
Please bring, gauze, tape, and three large boxes.
Please bring gauze, tape, and three, large boxes.
Please bring gauze, tape, and, three large boxes.
test.why: Commas separate the three items; “three large boxes” is cumulative, so it takes no comma.

whyNot.1: No comma goes between a verb and the first item it introduces.
whyNot.2: “Three large” is cumulative, so no comma between them.
whyNot.3: No comma goes after the conjunction “and.”
